rendered:
Short answer: the paper reports no leaching of nickel, manganese or cobalt into the Cyrene, and it gives no amounts for them. It says the relative Ni, Mn and Co ratios stayed the same before and after separation, which shows the process does not leach those metals.[1][2] The paper says the ICP-OES results supporting this are shown in Table S1. That table is not part of this document, so no concentrations can be read from it.[3][4] The only nickel, manganese and cobalt values in the paper are EDX mass percentages for the recovered NMC622 powder in Fig. 3[5] (panel e): Mn 13.36[6], Co 8.31[7], Ni 28.59[8]. These measure the solid surface, not the amount dissolved into the solvent.

Why the ether groups matter: the paper does not link Ni, Mn or Co to the ether groups. It links lithium leaching to them. It notes that lithium leaching from NMC622[9] occurred after recovery, and explains the cause as follows. The Cyrene molecule has ether groups, which attract lithium cations because ether is electron-donating. The paper says this causes lithium leaching and makes the high-Ni cathode more unstable.[10][11][12]
